chib-043.title: Neanderthals emerge in Europe
chib-043.text: Europe's most famous ancient people took shape slowly. Neanderthals had evolved by about 350,000 years ago, from Middle Pleistocene ancestors like those at Sima de los Huesos. Their distinctive teeth had appeared by about 300,000 years ago. From then on they lived across Europe and the Near East. Yet some Neanderthal traits appeared only near the start of the Late Pleistocene, perhaps when the species fully split off from its relatives.

chib-045.title: The Whakamaru supereruption shakes New Zealand
chib-045.text: About 340,000 years ago, New Zealand's North Island suffered a VEI 8 eruption sequence that lasted under a thousand years. It produced 1,200 to 2,000 km³ of tephra, the fragments a volcano hurls out. The collapse left the Whakamaru Caldera, about 30 by 40 km, just north of today's Lake Taupō. This was only the start. In a burst of under 100,000 years, the Taupō Volcanic Zone went on to erupt over 4,000 km³ in total. That burst belonged to an ignimbrite flare-up lasting from about 350,000 to 240,000 years ago.

chib-046.title: MIS 9, the Purfleet interglacial
chib-046.text: Between about 337,000 and 300,000 years ago came a warm spell called MIS 9, the Purfleet Interglacial in Britain. It was the last period of the Lower Paleolithic, the oldest stage of the Stone Age. Carbon dioxide was probably higher than in MIS 11. Even East Antarctica felt it. The Wilkes Basin there lost enough ice to raise sea level by about 0.9 m.

chib-047.title: The Schöningen spears, oldest complete wooden weapons
chib-047.text: Ten spears of spruce and pine lay in a lignite mine at Schöningen, Germany, beside butchered horse bones. They are the oldest complete wooden weapons known. Made by Homo heidelbergensis or early Neanderthals, they were probably used both for throwing and thrusting. They point to skilled hunting and planning ahead. Their age is disputed. They were first put at 400,000 to 380,000 years, then 337,000 to 300,000 by thermoluminescence. A 2025 study says about 200,000 years.

chib-048.title: Homo naledi in the Rising Star Cave
chib-048.text: Deep in South Africa's Rising Star Cave lay more than 1,500 bones from at least 15 individuals. They make up the largest find of a single hominin species in Africa. The species, Homo naledi, had a brain so small that its fossils were first assumed to be 1 to 2 million years old. In fact it lived there between 335,000 and 236,000 years ago, in the Middle Pleistocene. Its line had branched from other Homo by 900,000 years ago. The bones lie in the remote Dinaledi Chamber. Some researchers suggest Homo naledi deliberately placed its dead there, a claim still debated.

chib-049.title: New ways of living at Olorgesailie
chib-049.text: In Kenya's Olorgesailie basin, behavior changed when the land did. After a long stable spell, the local environment grew more variable around 400,000 years ago, as tectonic movement broke up the landscape. By about 320,000 years ago, people there moved obsidian over long distances, used pigments and possibly made projectile points. That timing roughly matches the earliest Homo sapiens fossils, suggesting complex behavior began with our species.

chib-050.title: The Levallois technique: planning a stone tool
chib-050.text: A Levallois toolmaker shaped a stone core first, then struck off a flake of a planned shape. This prepared-core technique was more elaborate than Acheulean methods. In Europe the Mousterian industry, built on it, appeared around 320,000 years ago and displaced the Acheulean there by about 125,000 years ago. Levallois-type tools occur in Levantine cave layers dated 250,000 to 140,000 years ago. By around 200,000 years ago the method was established among Middle Paleolithic toolmakers.

chib-051.title: Jebel Irhoud and the earliest Homo sapiens
chib-051.text: Bones from a Moroccan hillside pushed the origin of our species back by a hundred thousand years. The fossils from Jebel Irhoud were once thought to be Neanderthal. They are now assigned to Homo sapiens, with a weighted average age of 315,000 years. Burnt flint tools found with them were dated by thermoluminescence, a measure of when the stone was last heated, to about 315,000 years ago as well. They are by far the oldest known members of our species. They show that modern humans lived across Africa 100,000 years earlier than once thought. Homo sapiens arose in Africa from a lineage close to early {{ref:chib-017}}. Rather than coming from one cradle, early Homo sapiens may have spread across Africa, with several regions contributing. The Florisbad skull from South Africa, about 259,000 years old, is another early member of the species.

chib-052.title: The Middle Stone Age begins
chib-052.text: Around 300,000 years ago, Africa's Middle Stone Age began. It is linked to anatomically modern or nearly modern Homo sapiens. Its European counterpart, the Middle Paleolithic, broadly spans 300,000 to 50,000 years ago, so the Chibanian straddles the shift from the Lower to the Middle Paleolithic. Hafting, fixing stone points to handles, becomes much more common in both Europe and Africa after 300,000 years ago. By about 164,000 years ago at Pinnacle Point, South Africa, people cooked shellfish and heated silcrete, a hard rock, in fire to make it flake better into tools.

chib-053.title: Gigantopithecus, the giant ape, dies out
chib-053.text: A giant Asian ape, a relative of the orangutan, made its last stand in southern China. Gigantopithecus lived in central and southern China from about 2 million years ago. After about 400,000 years ago it survived only in Guangxi. Its youngest remains, from Shuangtan and Gongjishan Caves, are 295,000 to 215,000 years old. Subtropical forest was retreating, and that, perhaps with archaic humans, likely drove it extinct.

chib-054.title: Denisovans in Siberia and Tibet
chib-054.text: Most of what is known about the Denisovans comes from dirt and DNA. People left early Middle Paleolithic tools, including cores and scrapers, in Denisova Cave, Siberia, about 287,000 years ago. Denisovan DNA in the cave's sediments goes back to 217,000 years ago. A Denisovan molar about 200,000 years old carries about 5% of its genome from a previously unknown Neanderthal population. Child hand- and footprints at Quesang in Tibet, dated 226,000 to 169,000 years ago, may be Denisovan. They are the oldest human traces on the plateau. Denisovans ranged across Asia from about 200,000 to 32,000 years ago.

chib-055.title: A possible first exodus of Homo sapiens
chib-055.text: Our species may have left Africa long before its famous later dispersal. Early Homo sapiens, or a close relative, may have first left as early as 270,000 years ago, the first of several waves. The clue is genetic: Neanderthal mitochondrial genomes are closer to Homo sapiens than to Denisovans. Neanderthal genes in living people come from at least two episodes of interbreeding outside Africa, the first about 250,000 years ago.

chib-056.title: MIS 7, a cool interglacial in three pulses
chib-056.text: MIS 7, lasting from about 245,000 to 190,000 years ago, was a warm stage with three phases of very low ice volume and high temperatures. The warmest, MIS 7e, peaked about 237,000 to 228,000 years ago. Even so, it was the coldest interglacial since the Mid-Brunhes Event, with MIS 7e about 1.4 °C below pre-industrial global temperature. Its start, Termination III about 243,000 years ago, included a sudden cold reversal like the much later Younger Dryas.

chib-057.title: The Mamaku eruption forms Rotorua's caldera
chib-057.text: About 240,000 years ago, a VEI 7 eruption in New Zealand hurled out more than 340 km³ of rhyolitic Mamaku ignimbrite. As its magma chamber emptied, the ground collapsed into the Rotorua Caldera. Within days or weeks a second eruption from the same magma body burst out at Ohakuri, about 30 km south. The sequence formed the basin that holds Lake Rotorua.

chib-058.title: A sinkhole trap for mammoths in South Dakota
chib-058.text: Near Hot Springs, South Dakota, a limestone cavern collapsed into a steep sinkhole at least 20 m deep. A warm artesian pond, fed by groundwater rising under pressure, filled it. Its sediments buried Pleistocene animals, including 58 Columbian and 3 woolly mammoths. Luminescence dating in 2026 put the sinkhole's formation at about 232,000 to 160,000 years ago, in MIS 7 and 6.

chib-059.title: The last mesotheriids of South America
chib-059.text: South America's native hoofed mammals, the notoungulates, were dwindling. Mesotherium, the last mesotheriid and the last of the group called Typotheria, has its final records around 220,000 years ago. After it, Toxodontidae was the only notoungulate family to survive into the Late Pleistocene.

chib-060.title: Mitochondrial Eve, the oldest maternal line
chib-060.text: Every living person's mitochondrial DNA, passed only from mothers, traces back to one woman. Studies put this earliest maternal lineage of Homo sapiens at about 200,000 years ago. They point to the Makgadikgadi lake region of southern Africa as the homeland, followed by expansion about 70,000 years later. That homeland claim remains controversial. Another estimate puts Mitochondrial Eve at 99,000 to 148,000 years ago and the Y-chromosome ancestor at 120,000 to 156,000, both in Africa.

chib-061.title: Woolly mammoths take over from steppe mammoths
chib-061.text: In the mid-to-late Middle Pleistocene, the woolly mammoth replaced its forerunner, the steppe mammoth Mammuthus trogontherii. In Europe the takeover was complete by around 200,000 years ago. Neanderthals lived alongside these animals and used their bones for tools and building. At La Cotte de St Brelade, about 200,000 years ago, they did just that. In North America, woolly mammoths were among the northern specialists that spread south of Alaska with bison during the Rancholabrean.

chib-062.title: Early modern humans at Omo and Herto
chib-062.text: For decades, the oldest known Homo sapiens came from Ethiopia. The Omo Kibish remains, about 195,000 years old, long held that title. They supported an East African origin of modern humans around 200,000 years ago. Herto Man, also from Ethiopia and about 160,000 years old, adds further physical evidence from the Middle Stone Age.

chib-063.title: Steppe bison cross into North America
chib-063.text: The American bison descends from immigrants. Steppe bison crossed the Bering land bridge into North America around 195,000 to 135,000 years ago. Their arrival is so distinctive that it defines a new stage of the fossil record, the Rancholabrean, marked by the presence of Bison. They first appeared in northwestern North America during the Illinoian glaciation. Then they spread across the continent in the warm Sangamonian. They expanded south of Alaska with other northern animals: caribou, muskoxen, moose and woolly mammoths.

chib-064.title: The Penultimate Glacial Period, MIS 6
chib-064.text: The ice age before the last one was in some ways the harsher. The Penultimate Glacial Period ran from about 194,000 years ago, as the MIS 7 interglacial ended, to about 135,000 years ago. Its peak, around 140,000 years ago, brought Eurasia's most extensive glaciation in 400,000 years. A thick ice sheet over northern Europe slashed plant cover. High latitudes were colder than at the later Last Glacial Maximum, while the tropics were warmer. It is the coldest, final part of the Saale and Wolstonian complex. In North America the Illinoian Stage matches it, and the Bull Lake glaciation of the Rocky Mountains, about 200,000 to 130,000 years ago, ran at the same time.

chib-065.title: A jawbone in Misliya Cave
chib-065.text: A jawbone with eight teeth from Misliya Cave on Mount Carmel may belong to Homo sapiens. In 2018 it was dated to 177,000 years ago. If so, modern humans may have moved in and out of the Levant several times, possibly even before 200,000 years ago. A 210,000-year-old skull fragment from Apidima Cave, Greece, has also been read as Homo sapiens, though that idea has limited recognition.

chib-066.title: Karymsky blankets Kamchatka in ash
chib-066.text: About 177,000 years ago, a huge eruption spread ash over more than 1.5 million km². It has been linked to Karymsky volcano on the Kamchatka peninsula. The blast rated VEI 6 or larger.

chib-067.title: A second megaflood makes Britain an island
chib-067.text: The chalk ridge between England and France had already been breached once. During the Saalian, or Wolstonian, glaciation of MIS 6, a second megaflood finished the job. A lake held back in the Doggerland region of the North Sea burst through and cut the Strait of Dover. Cohen and Hijma date the ridge's final destruction to the Saalian peak around 160,000 years ago. The episode ended with a second meltwater lake about 130,000 years ago. Ever since, Britain has been an island whenever sea level was high.

chib-068.title: Megadroughts grip tropical Africa
chib-068.text: From 135,000 years ago, megadroughts struck tropical Africa. They pushed humans toward the coasts and onto other continents. By the MIS 5 megadrought, 130,000 years ago, Africa held two ancestral human population clusters. One of them, in the south, carried the maternal lineage known as mitochondrial haplogroup L0.

chib-069.title: Termination II melts the penultimate ice
chib-069.text: The end of an ice age is messy. About 133,000 years ago a surge of meltwater, pulse 2B, sharply weakened the Indian Summer Monsoon. During a peak in sunlight between 133,000 and 130,000 years ago, meltwater from the Dnieper and Volga poured in and joined the Black and Caspian Seas. This deglaciation, Termination II, also included a sudden cold reversal like the Younger Dryas.

chib-070.title: The Aso-3 eruption in Japan
chib-070.text: Japan's Aso caldera was carved by four great pyroclastic-flow eruptions between 270,000 and 90,000 years ago. Aso-3, about 130,000 years ago, produced about 96 km³ of magma, measured as dense-rock equivalent, the volume as solid rock. The earlier Aso-1, about 266,000 years ago, and Aso-2, about 141,000 years ago, each erupted about 32 km³.

chib-071.title: Burials at Krapina
chib-071.text: At Krapina in Croatia, the dead were buried about 130,000 years ago. Some anthropologists see in such burials a growing concern for the dead and a developing belief in an afterlife.

chib-017.title: Homo heidelbergensis, the muddle in the middle
chib-017.text: About 600,000 years ago in Africa, a new kind of human evolved from Homo erectus. Homo heidelbergensis is known from fossils of the MIS 15 interglacial, 621–563 ka, including Heidelberg Man and the Bodo cranium. It was the likely ancestor of Denisovans and Neanderthals, and perhaps of modern humans too. Some scholars place the first symbolic communication with this species. Yet it is a controversial, poorly defined species, and its classification is disputed. The tangle of Middle Pleistocene human forms is nicknamed the 'muddle in the middle'.

reviews.chibanian-age: The Chibanian began with Earth's last magnetic flip and ended in the meltwater of Termination II. In between, the ice ages beat to the new 100,000-year rhythm, swinging from giant glaciations like MIS 12 and MIS 6 to the long, warm MIS 11, and those swings broke Britain from France in two megafloods. Animals adjusted: woolly mammoths replaced steppe mammoths, bison crossed into North America, and the mammoth steppe spread with each cold spell. The human family branched too: Neanderthals and Denisovans parted from each other, while Homo sapiens appeared at Jebel Irhoud about 315,000 years ago. Fire became a daily tool, spears and Levallois cores showed planning, and burials at Krapina hinted at a concern for the dead.
